summary.title: The Practical Test Pyramid
summary.one_liner: Learn how to apply the test pyramid to split automated tests into unit, integration, contract, UI and end-to-end layers, with Java/Spring Boot examples.
keywords: how many tests should i write at each layer
takeaways: The test pyramid groups tests by granularity; write many fast unit tests, fewer integration/coarser tests, and very few end-to-end tests.
Unit tests should check observable behaviour via the public interface rather than internal structure, so refactoring does not break them.
Use the Arrange, Act, Assert (or given/when/then) structure to keep tests consistent and readable.
Integration tests cover one integration point at a time (database, REST API, filesystem, queues) and are needed wherever data is serialized or deserialized.
Layer names in the pyramid are flexible; keep them consistent within your codebase and team.
summary.summary: Martin Fowler's article revisits Mike Cohn's test pyramid and explains how to apply it in practice. It walks through a sample Spring Boot microservice with a REST interface, database and third-party weather API, and shows example tests at each layer, starting with unit tests written in JUnit and Mockito. It then covers integration tests for database and REST boundaries, and the article's table of contents also lists contract, UI, end-to-end, acceptance and exploratory testing, pipeline placement, and test code cleanliness. The text provided ends partway through the integration tests section, so the later sections were not visible here.
